Bias-corrected GLMs with misclassified covariates: mcglm() and mclm()

Maciej Beresewicz, Michal Warmuz

2026-05-08

Source: vignettes/mcglm.Rmd
mcglm.Rmd

Scope

This vignette describes the analytical bias-correction estimators in mismeasured: mcglm() for any supported family and mclm(), the Gaussian-fixed wrapper of mcglm(). Five estimators are implemented for GLMs in which a discrete covariate is observed only through a misclassified proxy: naive, additive bias correction (BCA), multiplicative bias correction (BCM), corrected score (CS, two formulations), and a one-step joint mixture-likelihood estimator.

For simulation-extrapolation methods, see the companion vignette vignette("simex", "mismeasured").

Setup and notation

Let YiY_i be a scalar response, xi∈ℝrx_i \in \mathbb{R}^r a vector of cleanly observed covariates (typically including an intercept), and Zi∈{0,1,…,K−1}Z_i \in \{0, 1, \dots, K-1\} a latent categorical regressor observed only through a proxy Ẑi\hat Z_i. For binary problems (K=2K = 2) take ξi=(Zi,xi⊤)⊤\xi_i = (Z_i, x_i^\top)^\top and ξ̂i=(Ẑi,xi⊤)⊤\hat\xi_i = (\hat Z_i, x_i^\top)^\top; for K≥3K \ge 3, ZiZ_i is dummy-encoded with baseline 00 so ξi=(di⊤,xi⊤)⊤\xi_i = (d_i^\top, x_i^\top)^\top. The parameter is ψ=(γ⊤,α⊤)⊤\psi = (\gamma^\top, \alpha^\top)^\top with γ∈ℝK−1\gamma \in \mathbb{R}^{K-1} on the (dummy-coded) latent regressor and α∈ℝr\alpha \in \mathbb{R}^r on xix_i.

The conditional mean is 𝔼[Yi∣Zi,xi]=μ(ψ⊤ξi)\mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i, x_i] = \mu(\psi^\top \xi_i) for μ=g−1\mu = g^{-1} the inverse canonical link.

Misclassification mechanism. For K=2K = 2 this is summarized by p01=Pr⁡(Ẑ=1∣Z=0)p_{01} = \Pr(\hat Z = 1 \mid Z = 0), p10=Pr⁡(Ẑ=0∣Z=1)p_{10} = \Pr(\hat Z = 0 \mid Z = 1), and prevalence π=Pr⁡(Z=1)\pi = \Pr(Z = 1). For K≥3K \ge 3, by the K×KK \times K column-stochastic matrix Πjℓ=Pr⁡(Ẑ=j∣Z=ℓ)\Pi_{j\ell} = \Pr(\hat Z = j \mid Z = \ell) and the prevalence vector (π0,…,πK−1)(\pi_0, \dots, \pi_{K-1}). We assume nondifferential misclassification: $\hat Z_i \,\rule[1pt]{8pt}{0.4pt}\!\!\!\rule[-3pt]{0.4pt}{8pt}\rule[1pt]{8pt}{0.4pt}\!\!\!\rule[-3pt]{0.4pt}{8pt}\, (Y_i, x_i) \mid Z_i$.

The naive proxy-score estimator and its bias

The naive estimator solves the proxy-score equation Ûn(ψ)=1n∑i=1nξ̂i{Yi−μ(ψ⊤ξ̂i)}=0. \hat U_n(\psi) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \hat\xi_i \{Y_i - \mu(\psi^\top \hat\xi_i)\} = 0. This is just GLM estimation with Ẑi\hat Z_i in place of ZiZ_i. It is typically inconsistent for ψ0\psi_0. For binary ZZ, the package theory (Warmuz & Beresewicz, 2026, Proposition on score drift) shows 𝔼[Ûn(ψ0)]=𝔼[mi(ψ0)], \mathbb{E}[\hat U_n(\psi_0)] = \mathbb{E}[m_i(\psi_0)], where the per-observation drift is mi(ψ)=(−c1δi(ψ)−c2δi(ψ)xi),δi(ψ)=μ(γ+α⊤xi)−μ(α⊤xi), m_i(\psi) = \begin{pmatrix} -c_1\, \delta_i(\psi) \\ -c_2\, \delta_i(\psi)\, x_i \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \delta_i(\psi) = \mu(\gamma + \alpha^\top x_i) - \mu(\alpha^\top x_i), with constants c1=p01(1−π)c_1 = p_{01}(1-\pi) and c2=p01(1−π)−p10πc_2 = p_{01}(1-\pi) - p_{10}\pi. The multicategory version replaces (δi,c1,c2)(\delta_i, c_1, c_2) with explicit double sums over (Π,πz)(\Pi, \pi_z) (Appendix B of the package theory note).

The five estimators

Method Idea Required nuisance Asymptotic regime
naive proxy GLM, no correction – inconsistent under fixed Π\Pi
bca additive: ψ̂bca=ψ̂−Î(ψ̂)−1m̂(ψ̂)\hat\psi_{\mathrm{bca}} = \hat\psi - \hat I(\hat\psi)^{-1}\hat m(\hat\psi) (c1,c2)(c_1, c_2) or (Π,π)(\Pi, \pi) drifting Π=O(n−1/2)\Pi = O(n^{-1/2})
bcm multiplicative: ψ̂bcm=ψ̂−(Î+M̂)−1m̂\hat\psi_{\mathrm{bcm}} = \hat\psi - (\hat I + \hat M)^{-1} \hat m same drifting Π=O(n−1/2)\Pi = O(n^{-1/2})
cs corrected score: solve ∑i[ξ̂i{Yi−μ(ψ⊤ξ̂i)}−mi(ψ)]=0\sum_i [\hat\xi_i\{Y_i - \mu(\psi^\top\hat\xi_i)\} - m_i(\psi)] = 0 same fixed Π\Pi
cs_akn AKN98 corrected score via unbiased surrogate x=Q−1(u−p0)x = Q^{-1}(u - p_0) Π\Pi only fixed Π\Pi
onestep maximize ∏i∑ℓπℓΠẑi+1,ℓ+1f(Yi∣Z=ℓ,ψ)\prod_i \sum_\ell \pi_\ell \Pi_{\hat z_i+1, \ell+1} f(Y_i \mid Z = \ell, \psi) via RTMB (see below) fixed Π\Pi

bca and bcm remove the leading n−1/2n^{-1/2} bias under a drifting-sequence regime where misclassification probabilities shrink with nn. cs and cs_akn are unbiased estimating equations under fixed Π\Pi – they remain consistent even when misclassification is moderate or large. onestep is a likelihood-based alternative implemented through automatic differentiation (RTMB); it estimates mixture weights jointly with ψ\psi unless fix_omega = TRUE.

Two CS formulations

The package implements two corrected-score estimators that solve the same population equation but differ in finite-sample form:

  • cs (drift) keeps the proxy as-is and adds the explicit drift mi(ψ)m_i(\psi) to the naive score. Needs (Π,πz)(\Pi, \pi_z). (Warmuz & Beresewicz, 2026, Theorem on the corrected-score estimator; Battaglia et al., 2025 for the linear-model origin.)
  • cs_akn (unbiased surrogate) transforms the regressor via x=Q−1(u−p0)x = Q^{-1}(u - p_0) where Q=[p1−p0,…,pK−1−p0]Q = [p_1 - p_0, \ldots, p_{K-1} - p_0], then substitutes into the log-likelihood. Needs only Π\Pi – πz\pi_z cancels out. (Akazawa, Kinukawa & Nakamura, 1998.)

The two are population-equivalent at ψ0\psi_0. Empirically they agree to ∼10−4\sim 10^{-4} for K=2K = 2 and within sampling noise for K≥3K \ge 3; cs_akn’s SD is slightly larger when Π\Pi has off-diagonals away from zero (the Q−1Q^{-1} amplifies single-observation contributions).

Inference

All five estimators report an asymptotic variance through vcov():

  • naive / BCA / BCM: A−1CA−1A^{-1} C A^{-1} where A=𝔼[μ̇(ψ0⊤ξi)ξiξi⊤]A = \mathbb{E}[\dot\mu(\psi_0^\top\xi_i)\xi_i\xi_i^\top] and C=𝔼[εi2ξiξi⊤]C = \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_i^2 \xi_i \xi_i^\top].
  • CS / cs_akn: J−1SJ−⊤J^{-1} S J^{-\top} with J=−(Î+M̂)J = -(\hat I + \hat M) (cs) or J=−IaknJ = -I_{\mathrm{akn}} (cs_akn) and S=𝔼[ϕiϕi⊤]S = \mathbb{E}[\phi_i \phi_i^\top].
  • onestep: inverse Hessian of the integrated log-likelihood.

Set vcov_corrected = TRUE in mcglm() to get a more conservative BCA/BCM sandwich that accounts for the additional uncertainty from estimating m̂(ψ̂)\hat m(\hat\psi).

Worked examples

Binary misclassification, Poisson response 

n  <- 5000
Pi <- matrix(c(0.9, 0.1, 0.1, 0.9), 2, 2)   # p01 = p10 = 0.10
z  <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.4)
z_hat <- z
z_hat[z == 0] <- rbinom(sum(z == 0), 1, 0.10)
z_hat[z == 1] <- 1 - rbinom(sum(z == 1), 1, 0.10)
x1 <- rnorm(n)
y  <- rpois(n, exp(0.8 * z - 0.5 + 0.7 * x1))

df <- data.frame(y = y, z = factor(z_hat), x1 = x1)

fit <- mcglm(y ~ mc(z, Pi) + x1, data = df, family = "poisson",
             method = c("naive", "bca", "bcm", "cs", "cs_akn"))
fit
#> 
#> Call:
#> mcglm(formula = y ~ mc(z, Pi) + x1, data = df, family = "poisson", 
#>     method = c("naive", "bca", "bcm", "cs", "cs_akn"))
#> 
#> Family: poisson  |  n = 5000, K = 2, p = 3
#> Methods: naive, bca, bcm, cs, cs_akn
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>         NAIVE    BCA      BCM      CS       CS_AKN 
#> gamma    0.6803   0.8182   0.8548   0.8554   0.8559
#> alpha0  -0.4362  -0.5043  -0.5223  -0.5265  -0.5253
#> alpha1   0.6906   0.6885   0.6879   0.6880   0.6849
#> 
#> Degrees of Freedom: 5000 Total (i.e. Null);  4997 Residual
#> Null Deviance:     9333 
#> Residual Deviance: 5605  | AIC (naive): 12610

The naive γ̂\hat\gamma is biased toward zero; all four corrections recover γ0=0.8\gamma_0 = 0.8.

Binary misclassification, logistic response 

n  <- 5000
Pi <- matrix(c(0.85, 0.15, 0.10, 0.90), 2, 2)
z  <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.4); zh <- z
zh[z == 0] <- rbinom(sum(z == 0), 1, 0.15)
zh[z == 1] <- 1 - rbinom(sum(z == 1), 1, 0.10)
x1 <- rnorm(n)
y  <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(0.9 * z - 0.4 + 0.6 * x1))

dfb <- data.frame(y = y, z = factor(zh), x1 = x1)
fitb <- mcglm(y ~ mc(z, Pi) + x1, data = dfb, family = "binomial",
              method = c("naive", "cs", "cs_akn"))
coef(fitb, method = "naive")
#>      gamma     alpha0     alpha1 
#>  0.6661615 -0.3362542  0.5299033
coef(fitb, method = "cs")
#>      gamma     alpha0     alpha1 
#>  0.9279532 -0.4041620  0.5409704
coef(fitb, method = "cs_akn")
#>      gamma     alpha0     alpha1 
#>  0.9276973 -0.4041227  0.5399984

Multicategory misclassification (K=3K = 3)

For K≥3K \ge 3 pass the misclassification matrix and (for cs/bca/bcm) the prevalence vector π\pi. cs_akn needs only Π\Pi.

n   <- 5000
Pi3 <- matrix(0.1, 3, 3); diag(Pi3) <- 0.8
pi3 <- c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2)
Z  <- sample(0:2, n, replace = TRUE, prob = pi3)
Zh <- vapply(Z, function(z) sample(0:2, 1, prob = Pi3[, z + 1]), 0L)
x1 <- rnorm(n)
ym <- rpois(n, exp(c(0, 1.0, -0.9)[Z + 1] + 0.8 - 0.7 * x1))

fit3 <- mcglm(ym, z_hat = Zh, x = cbind(1, x1), family = "poisson",
              method = c("naive", "cs", "cs_akn"),
              Pi = Pi3, pi_z = pi3)
coef(fit3, method = "cs")
#>     gamma1     gamma2     alpha0     alpha1 
#>  0.9974917 -1.2197661  0.8089698 -0.6927194
coef(fit3, method = "cs_akn")
#>     gamma1     gamma2     alpha0     alpha1 
#>  0.9985326 -1.2428888  0.8066988 -0.6920223

Confidence intervals 

confint(fit, method = "cs")
#>             2.5 %     97.5 %
#> gamma   0.7841097  0.9265936
#> alpha0 -0.5811827 -0.4717990
#> alpha1  0.6567124  0.7191898
confint(fit, method = "cs_akn")
#>             2.5 %     97.5 %
#> gamma   0.7845970  0.9272574
#> alpha0 -0.5803202 -0.4703317
#> alpha1  0.6521881  0.7176108

One-step (joint mixture likelihood)

The one-step estimator maximizes the integrated mixture likelihood across the latent categories. It uses RTMB for automatic differentiation and is robust under fixed Π\Pi for any KK. Mixture weights can be estimated jointly (default) or fixed at user-supplied πz\pi_z via fix_omega = TRUE.

fit_os <- mcglm(y ~ mc(z, Pi) + x1, data = df, family = "poisson",
                method = c("naive", "onestep"))
coef(fit_os, method = "onestep")
#>      gamma     alpha0     alpha1 
#>  0.8492809 -0.5019135  0.6972155

mclm(): Gaussian-fixed convenience wrapper

mclm() is a thin wrapper around mcglm() with family = "gaussian", in the spirit of base R’s lm() versus glm(). All other arguments forward unchanged and the returned object remains of class "mcglm", so all S3 methods (summary, vcov, confint, …) work identically.

n  <- 4000
Pi <- matrix(c(0.9, 0.1, 0.1, 0.9), 2, 2)
z  <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.4); zh <- z
zh[z == 0] <- rbinom(sum(z == 0), 1, 0.10)
zh[z == 1] <- 1 - rbinom(sum(z == 1), 1, 0.10)
x1 <- rnorm(n)
yg <- 0.8 * z - 0.5 + 0.7 * x1 + rnorm(n, 0, 0.5)

dfg <- data.frame(y = yg, z = factor(zh), x1 = x1)
fitg <- mclm(y ~ mc(z, Pi) + x1, data = dfg,
             method = c("naive", "cs", "cs_akn"))
coef(fitg, method = "cs")
#>      gamma     alpha0     alpha1 
#>  0.7913075 -0.4782274  0.6984542
coef(fitg, method = "cs_akn")
#>      gamma     alpha0     alpha1 
#>  0.7913625 -0.4782466  0.6998920

For Gaussian, cs_akn admits a closed-form linear-system solution (no iterative solver), so the two CS formulations agree to numerical precision.

When to use which method

  • Reliable (Π,πz)(\Pi, \pi_z), well-curated proxy. Any of cs, cs_akn, or onestep. Use cs for the most established formulation; onestep when you also want a likelihood-based confidence set or model fit comparison.
  • Reliable Π\Pi but πz\pi_z unknown or unstable. Prefer cs_akn – the surrogate construction makes πz\pi_z irrelevant.
  • Misclassification probabilities small and shrinking with nn. bca or bcm are valid (drifting-sequence regime). bcm removes second-order bias and is closer to the iterated CS update.
  • Multicategory K≥3K \ge 3. All five estimators apply; cs_akn carries a small variance penalty (≈ 10–20% larger SD) versus drift cs.
  • Multinomial response. Only naive and onestep (the others are univariate-response specific).

Estimated misclassification parameters

The package theory (Warmuz & Beresewicz, 2026, Proposition on plug-in robustness) shows that the corrected-score estimator remains consistent when (Π,π)(\Pi, \pi) are estimated from auxiliary data, provided the plug-in score satisfies sup⁡ψ∥Φn*−Φn∘∥=oP(1)\sup_\psi \|\Phi_n^* - \Phi_n^\circ\| = o_P(1), and is asymptotically unbiased under the tighter rate oP(n−1/2)o_P(n^{-1/2}). In practice this means a validation subsample of moderate size (e.g. 5–10% of the main sample) is sufficient.

Result object and S3 methods

mcglm() and mclm() both return objects of class "mcglm". The following S3 methods are available:

  • print(), summary() – coefficient tables per method.
  • coef(), vcov(), se(), confint() – accept a method = argument to select which estimator’s quantity to extract.
  • predict(), fitted(), residuals() – on the original (proxy) data.
  • logLik(), AIC(), BIC(), nobs() – only meaningful for onestep.

References

Akazawa, K., Kinukawa, N. and Nakamura, T. (1998). A note on the corrected score function adjusting for misclassification. J. Japan Statist. Soc. 28(1), 115–123. (Foundational existence theorem and explicit corrected scores for misclassified discrete covariates; basis of cs_akn.)

Battaglia, L., Christensen, T., Hansen, S. and Sacher, S. (2025). Inference for regression with variables generated by AI or machine learning. arXiv preprint arXiv:2402.15585. (Drifting-asymptotics framework for linear models; origin of BCA/BCM and one-step.)

Nakamura, T. (1990). Corrected score function for errors-in-variables models: methodology and application to generalized linear models. Biometrika 77(1), 127–137. (Originating reference for the corrected-score concept under continuous additive error.)

Warmuz, M. and Beresewicz, M. (2026). Bias corrections for GLMs with misclassified covariates. Working paper. (GLM extension of the drifting-asymptotics regime; multicategory drift formulas; plug-in robustness conditions used in the package.)
